papers.title: Triple jeopardy: trends in the co-occurrence of extreme heat, drought, and PM2.5 across the conterminous United States
papers.abstract: Abstract Compound climate hazards can produce risks exceeding those captured by single-hazard analyses, yet their joint behavior remains poorly characterized across the United States. Research has focused largely on drought-heat interactions, while growing evidence suggests other hazard combinations may increasingly shape population exposure. This study examines the co-occurrence of extreme heat, drought, and fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅) across the conterminous United States (CONUS) from 1991 to 2023, evaluating pairwise and triple interactions across multiple severity tiers. Rather than uniform intensification, results reveal a shift in the relative prominence of compound exposures. Heat-PM₂.₅ co-occurrence emerges as the most widespread and fastest-growing combination, averaging 22.7 days per summer at the mild tier, nearly three times the frequency of heat-drought, and increasing from 18.8 to 25.7 days per season (+36.8%) between the early (1991–2006) and late (2009–2023) periods. Significant monotonic increases occur across 64% of CONUS, compared with 0.3% showing decreases. Regional variation ranges from 6.8 days per season in the Western North Central region to 54.1 days in the Southeast. Heat-drought co-occurrence, by contrast, shows modest changes across most severity levels. Regional differences are pronounced in the South, exceeding 40 days per season, and the Northwest, where rapid increases coincide with expanding wildfire activity, although source-specific PM₂.₅ was not evaluated. Simultaneous co-occurrence of all three hazards remains rare, increasing from 0.02 to 0.10 days per season at the moderate tier against a 1991–2023 mean of 0.06 days. Despite this low absolute frequency, triple-hazard co-occurrence increases substantially in relative terms (+485% between periods), with significant increases across 18.1% of CONUS pixels. These findings indicate a reconfiguration of compound hazard exposure driven by the growing prominence of specific hazard combinations rather than uniform change, suggesting that frameworks centered on a limited set of hazard pairings may no longer capture dominant regional exposures.

papers.title: Predicting and Explaining Lightning and Lightning‐Ignited Wildfires in Northern California With a Two‐Step Convolutional Neural Network Framework
papers.abstract: Abstract Lightning‐ignited wildfires (LIWs) are a major contributor to burned area in Northern California and have increased substantially in size over recent decades. Predicting LIWs remains challenging because ignition depends on both lightning occurrence and fuel‐meteorology interactions. We develop a two‐step convolutional neural network (CNN) framework to conjunctively predict (a) lightning occurrence from meteorological conditions and (b) wildfire ignition conditional on lightning using both meteorological and fuel‐related predictors. The framework achieves skillful prediction, with testing accuracy of 0.82 for predicting LIWs. Explainability analyses using layer‐wise relevance propagation (LRP) reveal that the two‐step framework separates the dominant controls on lightning‐producing versus fire‐producing environments, highlighting the transition from synoptic‐scale instability and moisture patterns to locally receptive fuel conditions. Composite analyses across prediction outcomes further show that missed LIWs arise more often in “non‐typical” conditions, with high lapse rate but limited mid‐level moisture. Application to the 2020 Sonoma‐Lake‐Napa Unit (LNU) Lightning Complex fires demonstrates that the framework captures the large‐scale circulation favorable for lightning development and local fuel conditions conducive to ignition. These results demonstrate the value of separating lightning production from ignition processes and show how explainable machine learning can diagnose multiscale pathways and model failure modes associated with LIW.

papers.title: Ensemble fire probability prediction by integrating meteorological AI models with lightweight prediction networks
papers.abstract: Wildfires pose persistent threats to ecosystems and human safety, making timely fire-risk assessment essential for disaster prevention and resource management. However, conventional wildfire early-warning approaches are often constrained by static fire-weather indices or machine-learning models driven by reanalysis data, which cannot exploit future atmospheric fields. We therefore propose and evaluate a decoupled cascade framework that decomposes the problem into (i) an upstream AI weather model (Pangu-Weather) to generate future atmospheric states and (ii) downstream probabilistic fire classifiers. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to systematically compare the performance of three operational forecasting strategies (reanalysis, one-step forecast, and rolling forecast) for fire probability estimation. Using Africa as the study area, with multi-source data from 2014 to 2025, we find that one-step AI forecasts preserve the spatial fire-risk structure nearly as well as reanalysis data. Based on this dataset, we evaluated 11 downstream classifiers within a two-stage fire-occurrence and fire-intensity prediction design, while rolling forecasts suffer from degraded detection due to accumulated meteorological errors, with persistent reliability failure occurring after approximately six weeks. Cross-model consensus based on SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) identifies vegetation, land-surface conditions, and meteorological variables as robust contributors. Our results demonstrate that meteorological foundation models can serve as modular and interchangeable upstream modules for operational wildfire hazard estimation, offering a scalable alternative to end-to-end black-box fire foundation models.

papers.title: Land management to mitigate the risks of future fire in the Mediterranean region: strategies and barriers to their adoption
papers.abstract: Extreme wildfires are becoming more frequent in the Mediterranean region and already frequently exceed controllable thresholds, leading to large impacts on natural and social systems. Wildfire risk is predicted to increase in the region over the 21st century because of ongoing global climate changes. The risk of wildfires is being exacerbated by rural land abandonment, which is promoting increased landscape flammability; and by expansion of the wildland-urban interface. To address the challenges arising from fire regime changes, there is an urgent need to improve existing management strategies to reduce fire risk and to minimise the occurrence of extreme wildfires. Doing so successfully requires integrating insights across varied wildfire management paradigms, that stem from diverse disciplinary traditions and often serve competing policy priorities. Here we review the state of knowledge and practice on wildfire management in the Mediterranean region. We begin by highlighting the diversity of land management practices that deliberately or indirectly have been used for fire risk mitigation, shaping contemporary Mediterranean landscapes and fire regimes. We then summarise the evolution of policy priorities and fire management practices, and how these changes in infrastructural, economic and legal frameworks could influence landscape vulnerability to wildfire. We also examine some of the barriers that work against the adoption of management strategies to minimise wildfire risk at local and national levels. The paper brings together ecological, land-management, governance, planning and economic perspectives that are often treated separately, in order to clarify where current wildfire risk reduction strategies are supported by evidence and where important barriers remain. Finally, we integrate these different insights to identify key knowledge gaps and make recommendations for future action.

papers.title: Deadwood restoration in boreal forests benefits saproxylic beetles
papers.abstract: Forest management in Fennoscandia has nearly eliminated natural disturbances, such as fire, from forest ecosystems. This affects the composition of tree species, the availability of deadwood, and saproxylic beetle communities. Restoration methods such as prescribed burning and tree girdling aim to replenish the deadwood supply in boreal forests. Prescribed burning creates habitats that benefit fire-dependent beetles and influences successional patterns that benefit Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris). Tree girdling adds to already existing deadwood pools and provides a high variety in decay classes that benefit many generalist beetles. Both methods were applied at three treatment areas per method across three years (2022, 2023 and 2024) in Ekopark Ejheden, an area with a long history of fire. Deadwood volumes of six individual treatment areas, three for each treatment method and year, were calculated separately for snags and logs. Deadwood volumes, abundance, richness, diversity and composition values were used to compare between treatment methods. No significant differences in deadwood volumes were found. Deadwood abundance, richness and diversity were significantly higher in burnt plots at three years post-treatment than in girdled plots. Deadwood composition differed significantly between treatment methods and years. The indicator deadwood category composition showed that stands treated with prescribed burning produced logs and snags in intermediate decay classes. Stands treated with tree girdling produced logs in a wider range of decay classes, including very early to late decay stages. Ecletor traps were used to sample saproxylic beetles and abundance, species richness and diversity values were used to compare treatment methods. Beetle abundance and species richness were shown to be significantly higher in areas treated with prescribed burning than in tree girdled areas at one and two years post-treatment. Beetle diversity was significantly higher for prescribed burning at two years post-treatment. At three years post-treatment, no significant differences were detected. Beetle composition differed significantly between treatment method and time since treatment. Indicator species analysis showed 19 beetle species that were almost exclusively associated with prescribed burning and three species that were exclusively associated with tree girdling. My results show that both prescribed burning and tree girdling are effective tools for increasing the deadwood supply in boreal forests. Prescribed burning and tree girdling produce different deadwood categories, which can be interpreted in terms of how the methods act across the plot. Prescribed burning is shown to be clearly favoured by fire-associated beetle species, supporting the argument that fire as a disturbance is irreplaceable by any other method. Regardless of this, tree girdling is a valuable method for promoting the accumulation of deadwood in boreal forest ecosystems. This method should be regarded as an additional benefit rather than a replacement of prescribed burning.

papers.title: Localizable Climate Change Education in Schools: Examining Impacts on Students' Environmental Science Agency
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT As our daily lives become increasingly affected by climate change, school‐based science education plays a critical role in preparing students to understand and respond to this global crisis. This cohort controlled quasi‐experimental study conducted in the United States examined whether a localized climate change storyline unit compared to traditional instruction could enhance students' environmental science agency (ESA)—the sense of agency students feel when they can mobilize their scientific knowledge and expertise to act in their lives. We investigated localizable storylines, a curriculum design and implementation approach where secondary teachers author part of a climate change storyline unit with teacher‐designed locally relevant phenomena and local action projects. We assessed three dimensions of our ESA framework: sensemaking about climate change phenomena, students taking on roles in collective work, and foundation for change. Analysis of student outcomes ( n = 2062) revealed significant improvements in sensemaking about phenomena (dimension 1) with meaningful effect size ( g = 0.251) and enhanced foundation for change (dimension 3, g = 0.148) among intervention students. We found no significant differences for taking on roles in collective work (dimension 2). Exploratory mediation analyses indicated perceived relevance and perceived coherence mediated the intervention's impact on students' foundation for change. Importantly, positive effects appeared consistent regardless of students' initial climate change views, suggesting the approach transcends pre‐existing differences in climate change concern. This localizable storylines approach shows promise for serving as a scalable model to make localized climate change education more accessible to teachers and schools with consequential effects on students' sense of agency.

papers.title: Accountability to God, We the People and local government activism in rural Shasta County, California
papers.abstract: Political polarization is increasing globally through the rise of national actors further to the political right who often invoke faith-based values. In the United States, they argue for defending God-given unalienable rights and stewarding God's Kingdom on Earth. Local government increasingly is the locus of so-framed debates on policies from school curriculum to immigration and vaccination requirements. Efforts to reflect religious/faith-based beliefs in policies challenge the role of governance and are antithetical to decision making where separation between church/faith-based institutions and the state is long-standing. However, scant scholarly attention alongside rising conservatism at the local level has stymied our understanding in planning scholarship. In response, a novel conceptual framework is developed to guide research and analysis of faith fueled local activism and may align with broader political right efforts. It integrates religious studies, populism, social movement and planning scholarship. I present the case of conservative actors in rural Northern California's Shasta County, which is emblematic of broader trends in political right politics, polarization and faith-based motivations and influence, drawing upon in-depth interviews with respondents who largely identify as Christian and further to the political right and field observations. I find that local activism is interconnected with broader political right and faith-related U.S. efforts. Residents prefigure desired futures through policymaking engagement by creating civic opportunities and ecosystems of alternative news sources, education and governing. Interviewees recounted having direct callings from God and argued rights come from God, not government. This is in stark contrast to secularized society's norms. • Political right polarization infused with faith-based values is rising globally. • Local government increasingly is the locus of so-framed staunch contention. • Scant scholarship of religion and conservativism in planning stymies theorization. • A rural local California case emblematic of such polarization is analyzed. • Faith-based actors had significant impact anathema to secularized local governing.

papers.title: Study of Damage to Shutters Exposed to a Vegetation Fire: Definition of Vulnerability Thresholds
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the fire behavior of wooden, PVC, and aluminum shutters through laboratory and large‐scale experiments. Laboratory tests were conducted using a cone calorimeter to assess the ignitability of the PVC and wooden shutters, focusing on the critical heat flux of ignition, ignition time and critical Flux Time Product (). Additionally, field experiments on the EXPLORII platform were carried out to assess the damage caused to the three types of shutters when exposed to hedge fires. Key metrics such as heat fluxes, energies received, thermal dose, and FTP were analyzed to determine damage thresholds. The results revealed that aluminum shutters were the most fire‐resistant, withstanding peak of total heat flux of 177 kW m −2 without sustaining any damage. PVC shutters, on the other hand, showed deformation at low fire exposure, when there was no flame contact, that is, when the peak total heat flux was less than 50 kW m −2 . At these exposure levels, the wood shutters showed a greater fire resistance than the PVC shutters, with no damage below this total heat flux. When the flames came into contact with the shutters, resulting in the highest fire exposure, with a total heat flux above 50 kW m −2 , the trend observed previously was reversed, with wooden shutters suffering more damage than PVC shutters for a given total heat flux. Blackening and burning were observed on both shutter types. The study also evaluated the reliability of the FTP as an ignition criterion for wooden and PVC shutters.

papers.title: Conclusion
papers.abstract: This closing chapter reiterates some of the main messages from the volume by dispelling some common myths about climate mitigation. Myth 1. Factors other than greenhouse gas emissions have caused observed warming to date of 1.2°C . No. There is consensus among scientists that the warming to date above preindustrial levels (observed at weather stations and confirmed by satellite data) is from atmospheric accumulations of human-induced, heat-trapping gases, rather than other factors like changes in solar radiation and volcanic activity or urban heat absorption (see Chapter 2 ). Myth 2. Global warming is not a major concern because people can adapt, for example, by adopting air conditioning, drought-resistant crops, and moving to cooler climates . No. Global warming is causing a diverse range of climate risks such as greater frequency and intensity of heat waves, shifting precipitation patterns (which puts at risk water systems, agriculture, and ecosystems), droughts, wildfires, floods, and hurricanes—these risks are escalating because warming causes more energy and water vapor in the atmosphere. Higher atmospheric CO 2 concentrations also eat away at the minerals used by marine life to build their shells and skeletons. And there is an escalating risk of crossing (poorly understood) tipping points in the Earth’s climate system such as permafrost melting (which could turn on an unstoppable gas tap of CO 2 and methane), long-term collapse of major ice sheets (which could raise global sea levels several meters), changes in ocean circulation (which could radically change temperature and precipitation patterns around the world), and forest dieback (which could transform the Amazon into dry savanna) (see Chapter 2 ). Myth 3. Near-term mitigation action in advanced economies can largely get global emissions on track with temperature goals . No. Global emissions need to be cut 25–50 percent below 2019 levels by 2030 to get on track with limiting warming to 2°C and 1.5°C, respectively. This will not be possible without substantial emissions reductions in developing countries given they account for nearly 70 percent of global baseline CO 2 emissions in 2030 (see Chapter 2 ). Proportionate emissions cuts should however be larger in advanced economies, and international climate finance should support low-carbon energy transitions in low-income countries. Myth 4. The Paris process is on track for achieving global temperature goals . No. Even if fully achieved, current mitigation targets in Nationally Determined Contributions would only reduce global greenhouse gas emissions by 12 percent below 2019 level by 2030. Put another way, new measures equivalent to a global carbon price upward of $80 per ton are needed by 2030 to be on track with keeping warming below 2°C (the current global average carbon price is $5 per ton). If the required emissions reductions are not achieved by 2030, emissions will need to be cut even more drastically after 2030, rapidly raising the costs of low-carbon energy transitions and potentially putting temperature goals permanently beyond reach (see Chapters 2 and 9 ). Myth 5. Low-carbon technology subsidies and mandates can mimic many of the mitigation responses from carbon pricing . No. Carbon pricing can promote the full range of behavioral responses to cut emissions across fuels, sectors, firms, and households—and cost-effectively, because it equates the cost of the last ton reduced across responses. Low-carbon technology subsidies and mandates promote a much narrower range of responses. For example, in the power sector carbon pricing will reduce electricity demand, encourage operational efficiencies, promote switching from coal to gas and from fossil fuels to nuclear and hydro, adoption of carbon capture technologies, and switching from fossil fuels to wind and solar. In contrast, subsidies or generation share requirements for renewables promote only the last response. In addition, under technology subsidies and mandates there is no automatic mechanism for equalizing the cost of the last ton reduced across firms and sectors (see Chapter 3 ). Myth 6. Carbon pricing is not practical for developing countries . Not necessarily. Carbon taxes, that is, charges on the carbon content of fossil fuel supply, are a straightforward extension of fuel taxes, which are among the easiest of all taxes to collect and are well established in more than 160 countries. Alternatively, in energy-producing countries, carbon taxes can be integrated into existing fiscal regimes for extractive industries (combined with rebates/charges for exported/imported fuels). Emissions trading systems (ETSs) can be more administratively challenging, however, and may not be practical for capacity-constrained countries. ETSs require new capacity for monitoring emissions, given they usually apply downstream to emissions from power generators and industrial facilities. They also require supervision of allowance trading markets and enough participants to create fluid trading markets (see Chapter 3 ). Myth 7. ETSs are preferable to carbon taxes given the focus of mitigation targets on emissions rather than prices . Not necessarily. Carbon tax trajectories can be set such that projected future emissions are aligned with an emissions target for a given future year (perhaps with occasional interim adjustment). Trading systems can achieve annual emissions targets with greater certainty, but the flip side is uncertainty over future emissions prices which can deter low-carbon investments (whose lifecycle returns can be highly sensitive to future emissions prices). Indeed, trading systems are usually combined with mechanisms, like price floors and ceilings, to limit price volatility, sacrificing some of the certainty over emissions (see Chapter 3 ). Myth 8. Carbon pricing obviates the need for sector-based mitigation instruments . No. Leaving aside the possibility of sectoral mitigation targets and technology policies, sectoral-based mitigation instruments are still needed. This is because of likely constraints on the political acceptability of carbon pricing from its significant effect on energy prices, which in turn burdens households and firms. Complementary sectoral instruments should, insofar as possible, mimic the behavioral responses of pricing, while they avoid energy price increases and significant fiscal costs. Furthermore, extra high explicit, or implicit, carbon prices may be needed, even in the near term, to kick-start investment in certain hard-to-abate sectors if they are to be decarbonized by mid-century. For example, it is less costly to make new buildings net zero emissions (through insulation, electric heating, and rooftop solar), rather than building an emissions-intensive structure and subsequently retrofitting it to become net zero—and this may require strong upfront explicit or implicit carbon price signals (see Chapter 3 ). Myth 9. Low-carbon technology subsidies or mandates can substitute for carbon pricing when the latter is politically constrained . Not necessarily. There are more efficient alternatives to carbon pricing than low-carbon technology subsidies and mandates. In particular, feebates (sliding scales of fees/rebates on activities or products with above/below average emissions intensity) or tradable performance (or emissions rate) standards can cost-effectively promote the full range of behavioral responses for reducing emissions rates in different sectors, while they avoid both fiscal costs on the government (unlike low-carbon technology subsidies) and significant increases in energy prices (unlike carbon pricing). See Chapter 3 . Myth 10. Feebates and tradable performance standards (TPSs) require large numbers of firms . Not necessarily. Feebates can be applied when the number of firms (for example, in a particular industry like steel or cement) is small (or even one). The feebate specifies a pivot point emissions rate above/below which fees/rebates apply, and the pivot point is set exogenously by the government. TPSs do, however, require significant numbers to lubricate credit trading markets—if the number of participants is very limited, a feebate would be better in this regard. See Chapter 3 . Myth 11. Market-based mitigation instruments cannot be used for the power and industrial sector where governments are reluctant to significantly raise electricity prices or industrial production costs . Not necessarily. Feebates or TPSs can cost-effectively exploit all mitigation options for reducing the emissions intensity of the sectors. They do not raise government revenues, but they limit increases in electricity prices and production costs by avoiding charges on unabated emissions for the average firm. Capacity requirements for these instruments are, however, similar to those for ETSs and they do little to reduce electricity demand or industrial production levels (see Chapter 4 ). Myth 12. Subsidies for low-carbon technology adoption in industrial firms confer a large competitiveness advantage . Not necessarily. In quantitative terms, the effects of technology adoption subsidies on relative competitiveness are likely modest. The base of the subsidy is the emissions reduction, or a proxy for it, which is generally smaller than remaining emissions (the relevant base for carbon pricing), and the subsidy payment is at least partly offset by extra abatement costs. Auction mechanisms for allocating subsidies to lowest-cost bidders can also limit subsidy payments in excess of mitigation costs (see Chapter 4 ). Myth 13. Fuel taxes can promote decarbonization in transportation . Probably not. For many countries, fuel taxes may be at, or close to, maximum politically acceptable levels because of the unpopularity of higher taxes at the pump. And lifecycle costs (including fuel costs at current fuel taxes) are generally smaller for internal combustion engine vehicles than their electric vehicle counterparts—promoting transitions to the latter likely requires additional incentives. Rather than dramatically raising fuel taxes, this can be achieved with a feebate, which alters relative vehicle prices without a new tax burden on the average motorist. Yet they are increasingly threatened by wildfires driven by intensifying climate change and anthropogenic pressures. Despite this urgency, spatially explicit wildfire susceptibility assessments for arid oasis environments remain scarce. This study develops and validates a Fire Susceptibility Index (FSI) for the Lower Ziz Valley oases in southeastern Morocco using an integrated Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM) and remote sensing framework. Six conditioning factors were selected: Land Surface Temperature (LST), Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Normalized Difference Moisture Index (NDMI), proximity to roads and settlements, and land cover classified via a U-Net deep learning model (overall accuracy: 95%). Factor weights were determined through the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP; CR = 0.09) and aggregated using Weighted Linear Combination (WLC). Land cover (w = 0.30) and NDVI (w = 0.25) emerged as dominant controls, with anthropogenic proximity factors jointly accounting for 31% of the index weight. FSI values ranged from 0.30 to 0.91 (mean = 0.67), with 42.7% of the oasis area (~ 1,707 ha) classified as high susceptibility (FSI ≥ 0.7). Validation against the August 2021 fire event (318 ha) demonstrated strong predictive performance: 96.5% of burned pixels fell within high-risk zones, and mean FSI was significantly higher for burned (0.72) than unburned (0.67) pixels ( p < 0.001), with an AUC of 0.703. Corroborating validation against 60 historical fire records (2009–2024) showed that 98% of events occurred in high or extreme susceptibility zones. The resulting FSI map provides a robust spatial basis for prioritizing fuel management interventions and fire prevention strategies. Its integration into a dynamic geodatabase could further support the development of an early warning system (EWS) for operational wildfire prediction in these irreplaceable oasis landscapes.

papers.title: Drivers of post‐fire resprouting‐based resilience of co‐occurring species in Mediterranean SE Spain
papers.abstract: Resprouting is a major mechanism of post-fire persistence in Mediterranean woody plants, but quantifying its contribution to resilience is difficult when pre-disturbance data are unavailable. We assessed post-fire resprouting-based resilience in nine co-occurring woody species from southeastern Iberia and tested whether its drivers were consistent across species. We developed species-specific allometric equations from unburned individuals to estimate pre-fire biovolume. Resilience was quantified as the normalized biovolume recovery rate (NBRR), based on the ratio between post-fire biovolume measured 10-12 years after fire and estimated pre-fire biovolume. We then modelled NBRR as a function of microenvironmental conditions, fire severity, climatic niche position and plant size. Allometric models successfully estimated pre-fire biovolume and enabled resilience quantification. All species resprouted, and six exceeded their estimated pre-fire biovolume. However, resilience drivers varied among species. Environmental harshness reduced resilience in three species, fire severity increased resilience in four species under predominantly low-to-moderate severity, and larger pre-fire individuals generally showed lower recovery, whereas climatic niche position did not explain resilience. Plant-level biovolume modelling provides a practical framework to quantify post-fire resilience in resprouting species when pre-fire data are lacking. Strong interspecific variation in resilience drivers suggests that complementary responses among co-occurring species may enhance resilience at the community level.

We compiled 376 studies and extracted 4,379 pairwise relationships among drivers, pressures, abiotic states, and biotic states. Weather and climate, landscape factors such as topography, and agriculture were the most frequently studied drivers, with agriculture representing the dominant anthropogenic driver. Several drivers and pressures were poorly represented, including urbanization, recreation, water flow alterations, vegetation removal, and biological invasion. Abiotic research was concentrated on surface water chemistry and hydrology, while biotic research prioritized organismal metrics such as abundance, biomass, and vital rates over biodiversity metrics such as richness or community composition. The pathway with the highest number of statistical tests linked agriculture to contaminants, surface water chemistry, and biotic responses. Birds were the most frequently studied taxon and had consistent empirical support demonstrating their responses to agriculture, hydrology, wetland extent, and weather and climate, supporting bird abundance and vital rates as candidate indicators in agricultural landscapes. Plants were assessed less often, but existing statistical tests showed a high frequency of significant effects from agriculture, hydrology, substrate physicochemical conditions, and water chemistry, supporting plant abundance as a candidate indicator. Research effort was uneven across taxa, and research coverage did not consistently match the proportional distribution of human footprints to wetlands. This review identifies useful candidate indicators for wetland monitoring while highlighting where additional research is needed to reduce bias and inform conservation and monitoring. We also present an interactive web dashboard that allows readers to query the extracted Driver-Pressure-State relationships and explore the complete evidence base.

papers.title: ERF-LSFIRE v1.0: Coupling a Level-Set Fire Model with the Energy Research and Forecasting Model for Fire-Atmosphere Simulations
papers.abstract: Abstract. Wildland fire behavior is shaped by interactions among fuels, terrain, weather, and the lower atmosphere. Winds and fuel conditions control fire spread, while heat and moisture released by the fire can modify atmospheric stability and local winds, feeding back onto subsequent fire behavior. Here we present ERF-LSFIRE v1.0, a coupled fire–atmosphere modeling framework that integrates a C++/AMReX level-set surface-fire spread model based on the Rothermel formulation with the Energy Research and Forecasting model (ERF), providing a modular and scalable computational foundation for high-resolution coupled fire–atmosphere simulations. LSFIRE can be run standalone with prescribed winds or coupled to ERF in one-way and two-way configurations, with fire-generated sensible heat and moisture returned to the atmosphere in the two-way configuration. We verify the level-set implementation using analytical spread tests over flat and uniformly sloping terrain and demonstrate the coupled framework using simulations of the 2025 Palisades Fire in California and 2025 Cram Fire in Oregon. Standalone LSFIRE closely reproduces the analytical elliptical spread solutions. In the strongly wind-driven Palisades case, two-way coupling with ERF produces localized atmospheric perturbations but only modest changes in perimeter-scale spread. In the Cram case, where background winds are weaker and more variable, fire feedback produces larger near-fire perturbations and substantially alters fire progression relative to the one-way coupled simulation. These results demonstrate that ERF-LSFIRE provides a flexible framework for examining fire–atmosphere feedbacks and suggest that the influence of two-way coupling depends on the strength of fire-induced perturbations relative to the ambient flow. The framework also provides a basis for future applications involving wildfire impacts on energy-system operations and resilience.

This strategy alleviates the absence of labeled data, accelerates convergence, and creates strong optimisation. The training is performed based on a categorical cross-entropy loss using the Adam optimiser and supplemented by a dynamically scheduled learning rate that improves the adaptation of the gradients and stabilizes the optimisation process. For Dataset II, the model achieved an independent held-out test accuracy of 98.37%, with 483 of 491 samples correctly classified. papers.abstract: Abstract Climate change increases fire weather globally. Hot, dry and windy conditions raise the likelihood of fires igniting and spreading and make suppression more challenging. Each additional degree of global warming by 2100 adds approximately 270 days of extreme fire weather to the lifetime exposure of a person born in Portugal in 2025. The final output consists of a composite risk map implemented within an interactive WebGIS platform, designed as a reproducible and transparent decision-support tool to assist stakeholders in designing tailored civil protection plans. papers.title: A Spatial Database of Historical Fire in Westside Forests of the Pacific Northwest
papers.abstract: Recent fire activity across forests west of the Cascade Crest in Oregon and Washington (the “westside”) has increased interest in the region's historical fire regimes. Substantial spatial information exists describing the location, extent, and timing of historical fires in the region, but these records represent independent efforts at local-to-regional scales, with considerable variation in data resolution, methodologies, discoverability, and metadata. To address the need for a systematic dataset of historical westside fire, we compiled a spatial database of over 7,300 fire perimeters and burned areas covering 125,000 km2, sourced from 25 datasets including historical forest inventories, cohort age studies, fire atlases, and aerial photo interpretations. We provide metadata, documentation, and guidelines for applying and interpreting the database, as well as three case studies illustrating possible applications and potential limitations. While the database documents extremely large and well-known fires such as the Tillamook Burn and Yacolt Burn, it also points to the historical importance of smaller fires and patches of stand-replacing fire on the westside. The case studies demonstrate 1) historical variability in stand-replacing patch sizes during wind-driven fire events, 2) resilience to early 20th century fire along the North Santiam River of Oregon, and 3) the role of repeated fire in creating early seral landscape diversity in the Coast Range. By considering the strengths and weaknesses of individual sources and using multi-proxy corroboration to reduce uncertainty, this publicly available database provides opportunities for new insights into the geographic variability of historical fire regimes on the westside. Historical sources vary in spatial and temporal confidence, but can be used effectively by considering those limitations and finding corroboration in complementary data like aerial photography and field measurements. papers.title: Environmental and Human Nuclear Winter Risks in the Nordic Context
papers.abstract: Aerosols reaching the stratosphere from both nuclear war and volcanic eruptions can block incoming solar radiation, cool the planet, reduce light for photosynthesis, and in turn reduce food production, leading to regional and widespread famine. Similarly, Earth system models used to study climate effects of volcanic eruptions have been adapted for nuclear winter studies. For the Nordic mainland, the geographic location leads to disproportionally larger impacts than the global average for cooling and agricultural reduction under a range of nuclear winter scenarios, as is seen in the historical record after large volcanic eruptions.

papers.title: Magnitude and frequency of hurricane experiences shape community preparedness in distinct ways
papers.abstract: Prior hazard experiences can shape how communities prepare for future climate-related risks. Here, we examine this relationship by linking census block group-level wind and rainfall exposures from eleven storms affecting Louisiana during 2017–2021 with mobility-derived preparedness measures during Hurricane Ida (2021). We find that communities with prior exposure to higher-magnitude hurricane hazards, characterized by stronger winds and greater precipitation, exhibited higher preparedness levels. In particular, communities that had previously experienced hurricane-force winds (maximum wind speed ≥ 33 m s⁻¹) or extreme rainfall (≥150 mm in 24 h) showed substantially higher preparedness. By contrast, more frequent exposure to non-catastrophic winds (21–33 m s⁻¹) or rainfall (70–150 mm in 24 h) was associated with lower preparedness. These associations were stronger in communities facing higher forecast wind speeds and in coastal areas. Our findings reveal contrasting relationships of hazard magnitude and frequency with subsequent preparedness and highlight the importance of jointly considering both dimensions when designing targeted preparedness strategies. Communities impacted by prior catastrophic hurricanes exhibit better future-hazard preparedness whereas those exposed to frequent but non-catastrophic events show reduced preparedness, as suggested by a case study of Hurricane Ida (2021) integrating large-scale human mobility analysis with hazard modeling.

papers.title: Stakeholder perspectives on ecosystem services in truffle-producing systems: Insights from Spain
papers.abstract: Truffle-cultivating systems represent a distinctive type of Mediterranean agroforestry that combines high-value fungal production with open woodland management. While truffle cultivation has been widely studied from biological and technical perspectives, less is known about how stakeholders perceive the ecosystem services (ES) that it provides. This study investigates stakeholders’ priorities for provisioning, regulating and cultural ES in truffle-producing landscapes in Spain and explores how these priorities vary across stakeholders along a continuum of preferences, together with environmental worldviews. For this, we conducted an online survey using the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) to elicit ES priorities, while environmental attitudes of the respondents were obtained by employing the New Ecological Paradigm (NEP). In addition, we elicited stakeholders’ perspectives on the main constraints affecting truffle cultivation and the incentives for integrating intercropping systems into truffle production. Truffle production was ranked as the most important ES, reflecting the high economic value of this fungus, while wildfire regulation was the most valued regulating service. Stakeholder heterogeneity was characterised by a continuum rather than a neat separation between production-oriented and cultural-and-landscape-oriented preference gradients, though their separation was shallow and boundaries between them should be interpreted with caution. These differences were also associated with environmental worldviews: respondents more strongly oriented toward truffle production and fire regulation exhibited more ecocentric attitudes. Limited access to affordable irrigation was identified as the main constraint on truffle cultivation, whereas intercropping was primarily supported as a strategy for income diversification, with additional perceived benefits for soil quality. Overall, our results highlight truffle agroforestry as a financially viable pathway for delivering public ecosystem services in marginal Mediterranean regions. While exploratory, this study provides an initial, reproducible, stakeholder-based mapping of how ecosystem services, constraints and diversification options are perceived in this under-studied agroforestry system, offering basis for future more targeted assessments.

papers.title: From climate vulnerability to climate governance: a multi-hazard framework for adaptation planning evidence from Greece and implications for climate-sensitive regions
papers.abstract: Climate vulnerability assessments have traditionally focused on socioeconomic and demographic conditions as the primary determinants of regional resilience. However, the increasing frequency and intensity of multiple climate hazards challenge this perspective by revealing vulnerability patterns that cannot be adequately captured through conventional socioeconomic indicators alone. Although numerous composite vulnerability indices have been proposed, relatively few explicitly integrate climate hazards into a framework capable of supporting adaptation-oriented decision making. This study presents a multi-hazard climate adaptation framework that combines a Climate Vulnerability Index (CVI) with extreme- heat and wildfire- danger indicators to construct a Multi-Hazard Vulnerability Index (MHVI). The framework was applied to the 52 NUTS3 regions of Greece using official socioeconomic datasets together with ERA5 climate data for the period 2010–2023. Regions were subsequently classified using a two-dimensional quadrant typology based on the interaction between conventional socioeconomic vulnerability (CVI) and multi-hazard climate vulnerability (MHVI), defining four distinct vulnerability profiles. The results demonstrate that climate hazards substantially modify conventional vulnerability patterns, revealing significant regional differences that are not captured by socioeconomic conditions alone. Five regions were identified as exhibiting the Urban Thermal Paradox, whereby comparatively favorable socioeconomic conditions coexist with high multi-hazard climate vulnerability due to elevated exposure to heatwaves and wildfire danger. More broadly, the proposed typology shows that regions with similar socioeconomic characteristics may require fundamentally different adaptation strategies depending on the interaction between structural vulnerability and multiple climate hazards. Beyond improving vulnerability assessment, the proposed framework links spatial climate-risk analysis with differentiated adaptation priorities, providing a structured basis for evidence-based climate governance and adaptation planning. The integration of Earth Observation and geospatial information is further proposed as a mechanism for supporting the operational implementation of these adaptation priorities through continuously updated environmental monitoring. Although demonstrated using Greece as an empirical case study, the methodological framework may have broader applicability to Mediterranean and other climate-sensitive regions experiencing increasing exposure to multiple climate hazards, subject to further empirical testing.

papers.title: Sustained Livestock Grazing Enhances Soil Organic Carbon Storage in Sub‐Arctic Grassland
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Grazing systems remain under‐represented in global carbon cycle models, and grazed grasslands are rarely recognised as an active carbon sink. Emerging evidence indicates that grazing can enhance plant carbon allocation below‐ground, contributing to soil organic carbon (SOC) sequestration. Yet, long‐standing grazing practices are increasingly being abandoned in sub‐arctic regions with poorly understood consequences for SOC sequestration. Here, we examined the long‐term consequences of abandonment of livestock grazing for SOC in sub‐arctic grassland and heathland across 34 sites in Iceland, by comparing paired ungrazed exclosures (20–83 years) with adjacent continuously grazed land. Our results show that the cessation of grazing was associated with 8% lower SOC stocks in the topsoil (0–10 cm), but without effect on SOC in deeper soil. Overall, SOC stocks (on average 130 Mg C ha −1 in 0–60 cm) were an order of magnitude larger than carbon in total plant biomass, including roots, shoots and litter. With the cessation of grazing, root carbon and nitrogen stocks in the topsoil, as important factors of SOC dynamics, were 29% and 9% lower, respectively. Our findings indicate that soil nitrogen limitation associated with cessation of grazing promoted vegetation shifts from grassland into heathland or birch woodland at multiple sites. Both heathland and birch woodland were associated with markedly lower SOC stocks in the upper 30 cm of soil compared to grazed grassland. Therefore, we emphasise that sustained extensive grazing is important for maintaining SOC stocks of sub‐arctic grassland.

papers.title: Demining and revitalising war-affected landscapes in Ukraine: multi-actor governance responses
papers.abstract: Abstract Ukraine faces one of the world’s largest and most complex explosive-ordnance contamination problems, affecting agricultural land, settlements, forests, and other natural ecosystems. This paper examines how global demining strategies are adapted within Ukraine’s multi-actor governance system and what this means for linking clearance with land recovery, soil restoration, and long-term environmental resilience. It addresses a gap in understanding how mine-action governance supports integrated landscape recovery in war-affected settings. We developed a seven-strategy analytical typology of mine-action and land-recovery approaches, comprising manual clearance, mechanical demining, remote sensing and mapping, community-based approaches, ecological remediation, legal and institutional frameworks, and post-conflict land-use zoning. Applying this typology to Ukraine and drawing on stakeholder analysis, policy review, and expert interviews, we found that manual clearance and mechanical land-release methods remain central, yet supported by new legal, institutional, and governance arrangements. Digital innovation in Ukraine’s mine-action sector is advancing rapidly, with UAV mapping, AI-supported detection, and integrated prioritization platforms increasingly incorporated into survey and planning processes. Uptake remains uneven, however, and interoperability and data-sharing gaps continue to limit implementation. Ukraine’s mine-action governance system is multi-actor and polycentric, but coordination remains challenging because of overlapping mandates, fragmented information flows, and differing donor priorities. These conditions reveal both opportunities and coordination challenges in linking mine action to environmental recovery and long-term land-use planning. Environmental concerns, including soil contamination in and around explosion craters, damage to forest areas, and degradation of shelterbelts, are receiving increasing attention, yet implementation remains limited and often confined to small or time-bound pilot projects. Community participation in prioritization of mine-action activities remains uneven, and interviewees reported that smallholders risk being sidelined by larger agricultural actors with greater influence over clearance demands. Scale remains a major challenge, requiring coordination across national, regional, and local levels while reconciling different humanitarian, economic, environmental, and recovery priorities. Our findings highlight that sustainable recovery depends on integrating mine action governance, environmental assessment and remediation, land-use planning, and long-term soil and ecosystem monitoring into a coherent recovery process. Ukraine’s evolving multi-actor approach offers lessons for other conflict-affected regions seeking to address explosive-ordnance contamination, environmental degradation, and landscape and livelihood recovery during and after armed conflict.

papers.title: Dual-band information helps constrain canopy water content and temperature retrievals from vegetation optical depth
papers.abstract: Abstract. Vegetation canopy water content and temperature fundamentally control plant physiology. They usually have strong diurnal cycles with substantial variations on the hourly basis. However, due to the scarcity of high-frequency observations, a major obstacle has long been existing in deciphering the plant hydrodynamics. Vegetation Optical Depth (VOD) provides a promising satellite and ground-based proxy by quantifying microwave attenuation by canopy liquid water, but it co-varies with biomass and temperature. Temperature-dependent dielectric effects also complicate the isolation of water dynamics. To assess the information extent that can be inferred from VOD and to assess the contribution of a second wavelength (as available with Global Navigation Satellite System, GNSS) in disentangling influences from multiple processes, we developed a Bayesian inversion framework coupled to a semi-empirical electromagnetic model to retrieve canopy water content (Mg), vegetation volume, and canopy temperature from single- and dual-frequency data using both theoretical sensitivity analyses and GNSS observations. After testing with simulated VOD at two GNSS bands (1.575 and 1.176 GHz), we applied the method to in situ GNSS-based VOD and evaluated against field measurements. Simulations indicate that single-band VOD with 0.5–4% measurement error already constrains Mg and vegetation volume. Adding a second band substantially improves temperature retrievals, reducing posterior uncertainty to 2.3K, although the benefit declines rapidly as VOD errors grow. When applied to observations, incorporating scaled leaf area index as an additional constraint improves the Mg-leaf water potential relationship, underscoring the value of auxiliary information. Through a first direct comparison of the information provided by mono-band and dual-band, our results show that converting VOD into biophysical variables is strengthened by dual-frequency information and complementary constraints, emphasizing the need for additional validation to robustly retrieve canopy water content and temperature at high frequency.

papers.title: Effects of agroforestry practices on insect abundance, richness, and diversity, in transformed ecosystems of the semi-arid area, Dodoma, Tanzania
papers.abstract: This study investigated surface-active insect abundance, diversity, and community composition to evaluate the conservation potential of agroforestry in transformed semi-arid ecosystems. Agroforestry ranked second in abundance (28%, n=810) but had the lowest diversity and richness, with high species dominance driven by Pachycondyla tarsata . Bushland showed relatively low abundance but moderate diversity and evenness. Community composition analyses revealed a clear visual separation, but statistically insignificant differences in insect assemblages across habitats (NMDS stress = 0.068, F = 0.96, p = 0.546). By contrast, PERMDISP detected highly significant differences in dispersion (p < 0.001), demonstrating that within-habitat variability rather than habitat type per se was the primary driver of community structure. Regression models confirmed that afforested habitats significantly influenced higher insect abundance and diversity, whereas other habitats showed no meaningful differences. The findings suggest that agroforestry enhances insect abundance but supports fewer species and lower diversity than shrubland and afforested habitats. Conservation strategies in semi-arid landscapes should therefore emphasize maintaining habitat heterogeneity and structural complexity to stabilize insect communities and sustain ecosystem services.
